readings.title: A bedtime routine for shift workers
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A workplace offered a sleep workshop to employees on rotating shifts. Advice built around a nine-to-five day felt unrealistic to many participants. The main obstacle was guidance based on a single work schedule. Night workers had different light exposure and family responsibilities from daytime staff. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used anonymous diaries of work and rest. Educators asked employees when they slept and which routines were within their control. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated flexible principles were more useful than fixed hours. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced examples for several shift patterns. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: health advice should fit the lives it addresses. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a bedtime routine for shift workers, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Noise near student bedrooms
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A college dormitory received complaints about night noise. The manager first blamed the common room, but residents reported sound from the service door. The main obstacle was a noise source identified by assumption. The door closed loudly even when the common room was empty. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used evening observations at several locations. Staff recorded times and asked residents to identify where the sound seemed strongest. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated the door caused most repeated disturbance. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a quiet closer and clear late-hour reminders. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: a solution should target the actual cause. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in noise near student bedrooms, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: An evening screen-use discussion
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An adult learning group discussed screen use before bed. Participants had different experiences, and some relied on phones for family messages. The main obstacle was advice presented as a rigid ban. The initial leaflet ignored necessary communication and treated every device use alike. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a discussion of practical evening habits. The tutor invited adults to describe what helped them wind down without collecting private health data. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated small choices felt more manageable. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a menu of optional routines rather than one rule. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: personal routines are easier to change when advice is realistic. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in an evening screen-use discussion, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Planning a quiet room at a library
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library offered a quiet rest room during examination weeks. Demand peaked after lunch, but its opening schedule followed ordinary staffing hours. The main obstacle was hours that missed the busiest rest period. Students arrived just as the room closed for a staff break. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used an anonymous count of room visits. Librarians compared arrival times with requests at the front desk. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated a modest schedule change improved access. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a later break and clearly posted hours. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: wellbeing facilities need to match real use. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in planning a quiet room at a library, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the healthy routines education programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about sleep and daily routines, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关睡眠与日常作息的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the health education team suggesting a practical change to the healthy routines education programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the healthy routines education programme. People have noticed guidance based on a single work schedule, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
